lead: A large sample turns an average into an approximately normal quantity. That is the whole engine of this chapter: subtract the claimed value from the estimate, divide by the standard error, and compare the result with the normal tables. The same recipe tests a mean, the difference of two means, a proportion, or the difference of two proportions. It is used to check a supplier's claim on bulb life, a hospital's claim on a cure rate, or a firm's claim that two payment channels fail equally often.
prereq: You need: the normal distribution (Unit 3), the central limit theorem (Unit 4), standard error and confidence intervals (Unit 5), and the logic of 6.1.

blocks.text: A sample mean is a random quantity. If the population mean is μ0 and the population standard deviation is σ, then x̄ has mean μ0 and standard error σ/√n. When n is large the central limit theorem (Unit 4) says x̄ is close to normal, whatever the shape of the population.

blocks.where: x̄ is the sample mean; μ0 is the claimed population mean; σ is the population standard deviation (use the sample value s when n ≥ 30); n is the sample size. Under H0, z is roughly standard normal, so normal tables give the p-value.

blocks.text: Population σ is rarely known. For a large sample you may put the sample standard deviation s = √[Σ(xi − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1)] in its place; the extra error is small once n ≥ 30. That is the large-sample condition. Below 30 use the t-test of 6.3.
Decision rule: reject H0 when |z| exceeds the critical value. A two-sided test puts half of α in each tail. A one-sided test puts all of α in one tail, so its critical value is smaller.

sections.h3: Two means, and the interval link

blocks.text: Take two independent samples with means x̄1, x̄2, sizes n1, n2 and sample standard deviations s1, s2. Under H0: μ1 = μ2 the difference x̄1 − x̄2 has mean 0. Variances of independent quantities add, so the standard error is √(s1²/n1 + s2²/n2).

blocks.where: x̄1, x̄2 are the two sample means; s1², s2² are the two sample variances; n1, n2 are the two sample sizes. Both samples should be large. The test answers questions such as whether two warehouses have the same mean delivery time.

blocks.text: Confidence interval link. A two-sided test at level α rejects H0 exactly when μ0 falls outside the 100(1 − α)% interval x̄ ± z<sub>α/2</sub> σ/√n, where z<sub>α/2</sub> is the standard normal critical value for the chosen confidence level. For 95%, z<sub>0.025</sub> = 1.96. For the bulb case below, the 95% interval is 990 ± 1.96 × 5 = 990 ± 9.8, that is (980.2, 999.8) hours. The value 1000 lies outside it, matching the rejection. Reporting the interval as well as the verdict shows the size of the effect in hours, not just significance.

Count x successes in n trials and set p̂ = x/n. Test H0: p = p0 with the statistic below. The standard error uses p0, not p̂, because the test is carried out as if H0 were true. The normal approximation is adequate when np0 ≥ 5 and n(1 − p0) ≥ 5; some syllabi ask for 10 instead of 5.

blocks.where: p̂ = x/n is the sample proportion; p0 is the claimed proportion; n is the number of trials.

blocks.text: Two proportions. Under H0: p1 = p2 both samples estimate one common proportion, so pool them: p̂ = (x1 + x2)/(n1 + n2). Then z = (p̂1 − p̂2) ÷ √(p̂(1 − p̂)(1/n1 + 1/n2)). The two-proportion z-test needs the counts of successes and failures in both samples to be large enough; a common rule is x1, n1 − x1, x2, n2 − x2 each at least 5 (some syllabi say 10). Example: 40 of 500 Android users abandon a checkout, 30 of 400 iOS users do. p̂1 = 0.080, p̂2 = 0.075, pooled p̂ = 70/900 = 0.0778, standard error = √(0.0778 × 0.9222 × 0.0045) = 0.0180, and z = 0.005/0.0180 ≈ 0.28. No evidence of a difference. For a confidence interval of p1 − p2, use the unpooled standard error √(p̂1(1 − p̂1)/n1 + p̂2(1 − p̂2)/n2), because an interval must not assume H0.

figure.caption: The standard normal curve with vertical lines at −1.96 and +1.96. The two tails beyond the lines together hold 5% of the area; a computed z outside them is rejected at the 5% level in a two-sided test.

spec.aria: A standard normal curve with vertical lines at minus 1.96 and plus 1.96 marking the two-tailed 5% rejection region.

examples.question: A manufacturer claims the mean life of a bulb is 1000 hours. A sample of 100 bulbs gives a mean life of 990 hours. The population standard deviation is known to be 50 hours. Test H0: μ = 1000 h against H1: μ ≠ 1000 h at α = 0.05. Also give the p-value and the 95% confidence interval.
steps: State the hypotheses: H0: μ = 1000 h, H1: μ ≠ 1000 h. Two-sided test, α = 0.05, critical values ±1.96.
p-value: P(|Z| > 2.00) = 2 × 0.02275 = 0.0455, which is below 0.05, agreeing with the rejection.
95% confidence interval: 990 ± 1.96 × 5 = 990 ± 9.8, giving (980.2, 999.8) h. The claimed 1000 h lies outside, again matching.
examples.answer: Reject H0 at the 5% level: the sample mean of 990 h differs significantly from the claimed 1000 h (z = −2.00, p = 0.0455, 95% CI 980.2 h to 999.8 h).
examples.check:
import math
n = 100
mu0 = 1000.0
sigma = 50.0
xbar = 990.0
se = sigma / math.sqrt(n)
z = (xbar - mu0) / se
p = math.erfc(abs(z) / math.sqrt(2))
print(round(se, 4))
print(round(z, 4))
print(round(p, 4))
print(round(xbar - 1.96 * se, 4))
print(round(xbar + 1.96 * se, 4))

traps: Dividing by s instead of σ/√n — the denominator is always a standard error, so the √n must be there.
Using s with a small sample: if n < 30 and σ is unknown, the correct test is the t-test, not z.
Mixing the critical values: 1.96 is two-sided 5%, 1.645 is one-sided 5%. Check the alternative before choosing.
Putting p̂ into the standard error of a one-proportion test. Under H0 the standard error is built from p0.
Comparing two proportions without pooling. Under H0 both samples share one proportion, so the pooled estimate belongs in the standard error.

quiz.q: Write the one-sample large-sample z-statistic for a mean and state the large-sample condition.
quiz.a: z = (x̄ − μ0)/(σ/√n), with s used in place of σ when n ≥ 30. The large-sample condition is n ≥ 30.

quiz.q: Why does the one-proportion test use p0 in the standard error while the two-proportion test uses a pooled p̂?
quiz.a: Both tests evaluate the statistic as if H0 were true. Under H0: p = p0 the variance of p̂ is fixed at p0(1 − p0)/n. Under H0: p1 = p2 the two samples share one unknown proportion, best estimated from all the data by the pooled value, which then fixes the variance.

quiz.q: A sample of 64 parts has mean length 48.5 mm. The population standard deviation is 4 mm. Test H0: μ = 50 mm against H1: μ ≠ 50 mm at α = 0.05.
quiz.a: Standard error = 4/√64 = 0.5 mm. z = (48.5 − 50)/0.5 = −3.00. |z| = 3.00 > 1.96, so reject H0. The mean length differs from 50 mm.

quiz.q: In two cities, 60 of 200 households and 45 of 180 households use a service. Test equality of the two proportions at α = 0.05.
quiz.a: p̂1 = 0.30, p̂2 = 0.25. Pooled p̂ = 105/380 = 0.2763. Standard error = √(0.2763 × 0.7237 × (1/200 + 1/180)) = 0.0459. z = 0.05/0.0459 = 1.09. Since 1.09 < 1.96, do not reject H0; the difference is not significant.

quiz.q: A 95% confidence interval for a mean is (12.4, 15.6). A two-sided test at 5% is run with H0: μ = 16 and then with H0: μ = 13. Predict both verdicts without computing z, and explain.
quiz.a: For μ0 = 16: 16 lies outside the interval, so reject H0. For μ0 = 13: 13 lies inside the interval, so do not reject. A two-sided test at level α rejects exactly those values excluded by the 100(1 − α)% interval.

quiz.q: A student tests a mean with n = 25 and unknown σ by using s in the z formula and the value 1.96. Identify the two errors and state the correct procedure.
quiz.a: First, n = 25 is below 30, so the large-sample normal approximation is not justified. Second, with σ unknown the statistic (x̄ − μ)/(s/√n) does not follow a normal distribution; it follows Student's t with n − 1 = 24 degrees of freedom. The correct test uses the t distribution with 24 degrees of freedom, and the critical value is read from the t table, not 1.96.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry this same z logic appears as A/B testing: an online firm splits users into two groups and compares conversion proportions with the pooled formula above. The large-sample normal approximation is the basis of the Wald interval, and newer curricula replace it with the Wilson score interval when proportions sit near 0 or 1. Repeatedly checking a running test and stopping when it looks significant needs corrections this chapter does not cover. Search 'A/B test sample size', 'Wilson score interval' or 'sequential testing alpha spending' to go further.
